stem: A 6-year-old boy is scheduled for a non-urgent lumbar puncture on the paediatric ward. Which preparation plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Obtain consent with a full explanation and fact sheet, use a local anaesthetic patch on the lower back unless urgency is extreme, then position him on his side with his legs curled up under his chin
Rely on brief verbal agreement alone, omit the fact sheet, and position him flat with his legs extended
Use local anaesthetic injection routinely first because it improves landmark identification
Leave comfort measures until after needle insertion so the examination is not obscured
Use oral sucrose as the main comfort strategy because this is the preferred option for older children

explanation: The correct answer is to obtain consent with a full explanation and fact sheet, use a local anaesthetic patch on the lower back unless urgency is extreme, and position the child on his side with his legs curled up under his chin.

citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

rationale: This preserves the standard preparation for a non-urgent lumbar puncture: informed consent, age-appropriate explanation with written information, topical local anaesthesia when time allows, and lateral flexed positioning.

optionExplanations.A: Correct because it matches the described preparation: consent, full explanation and fact sheet, topical local anaesthetic patch unless urgency is extreme, and lateral positioning with flexion.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because brief verbal agreement alone is not adequate preparation, and the position described is not the recommended lateral flexed posture.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because the preferred approach is a local anaesthetic patch when time allows; routine injection is not the described first choice.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because comfort measures should be part of preparation before the procedure, not delayed until after needle insertion.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because oral sucrose is used for neonates, not as the main comfort strategy for an older child.
